texto.titulo: Peer feedback in academic writing: definitions, validity and approaches to improvement
texto.abstract: This article examines peer feedback in academic writing in higher education, beginning with the reasons why it has come to occupy a central place in writing instruction. Competing definitions of the practice are then compared, and the questions of validity and reliability on which its credibility depends are considered in turn. It is argued that the alternative labels proposed in recent years – ‘peer review’, ‘peer grading’ and ‘co-assessment’ – add little conceptual clarity and, in some cases, obscure the formative purpose of the practice. Five approaches intended to improve the quality of peer feedback are subsequently reviewed: rubrics, anonymous feedback, revision cycles, reviewer training and self-assessment. These are found to be complementary rather than interchangeable, and none of them is shown to guarantee useful feedback on its own.
texto.keywords: peer feedback, peer assessment, academic writing, validity, reliability, higher education

blocos.h2: The need for peer feedback in academic writing

blocos.p: It is often claimed that students learn as much from reviewing the work of their peers as from receiving comments on their own. Since the first syntheses on the subject appeared in the mid-2000s, peer feedback has been incorporated into writing courses across a wide range of disciplines, from first-year composition to doctoral seminars, and it is now routinely recommended in institutional guidelines on assessment (Consortium for Writing Pedagogy 2017). Its advocates point to a number of benefits: the development of evaluative judgement, the exposure of students to alternative ways of structuring an argument, a greater awareness of the needs of a reader, and a reduction in the workload of instructors who would otherwise be the sole source of comments on drafts. Ferrant (2006), in one of the earliest syntheses on the subject, adds that students who give feedback tend to revise their own texts more extensively than those who only receive it. Not all of these claims, however, rest on equally solid evidence, and several of them depend on assumptions about the quality of the comments exchanged which are rarely examined.

Three difficulties, in particular, have been identified. The first is that students frequently doubt the competence of their peers and, as a consequence, disregard comments which do not come from an instructor (Ilunga and Sorvik 2012). The second is that feedback produced without guidance tends to concentrate on surface features such as spelling, punctuation and formatting, leaving the argument and organisation of the text largely untouched. The third, and arguably the most serious, is that the comments a student receives may depend less on the qualities of the draft than on who happens to be assigned to read it. It is the last of these which has attracted most attention in the research literature, since it raises directly the questions of validity and reliability to which a large part of this article is devoted. Before these can be addressed, however, it is necessary to establish what is meant by peer feedback, a task which proves less straightforward than might be expected.

Taking three frequently cited sources, peer feedback can be described as ‘the exchange of written or spoken comments on a draft between students enrolled in the same course, with the aim of informing its revision’ (Ilunga and Sorvik 2012, p. 214). Castelnau (2015, p. 47) defines it more broadly as ‘any judgement about the quality of a text that is formulated by a learner and addressed to another learner’, irrespective of whether a revision follows. Oyelaran (2010), by contrast, insists that feedback exists only when the comments are acted upon: a remark which leaves the text unchanged is, in her terms, ‘information, not feedback’. At first sight these definitions appear to diverge considerably. On closer inspection, however, the divergence concerns the moment at which the process is considered complete rather than the nature of the process itself: all three identify a learner as the source of the comments, a text as their object and improvement as their ultimate purpose.

The prevailing understanding of peer feedback thus places the emphasis on its formative function. A number of authors nevertheless maintain that a summative component cannot be excluded. Rhydderch et al. (2018) argue that, wherever peer comments are accompanied by a mark which contributes to the final grade, the practice should be described as peer assessment, and they propose a continuum running from purely formative feedback, through mixed arrangements, to purely summative grading. Quennell (2014) goes further, contending that the formative and summative functions are inseparable in practice, given that students who know that a mark is involved write comments of a different kind from those who do not. These distinctions are useful, but they would appear to describe variations in the conditions under which feedback is given rather than different concepts. Whether or not a mark is attached, the activity consists in the same operation: a learner reads the text of another learner and formulates a judgement about how it might be improved.

A further line of definition emphasises the dialogic character of the practice. For Bakhtiyari and Lund (2017), feedback is not a product handed from one student to another but a conversation in which the writer is expected to respond, to ask for clarification and, where necessary, to reject the suggestions received. Their account draws on studies of writing groups in which drafts were discussed face to face, and it has been influential among instructors who regard the one-way transmission of comments as a residue of more traditional models of teaching. It must be noted, however, that most of the arrangements reported in the literature are not dialogic in this sense: comments are typically submitted through an online platform, read by the writer some days later and never discussed. Bakhtiyari and Lund do not deny that such arrangements exist; they simply decline to call them feedback, a position which, if accepted, would exclude the majority of the practices they set out to describe.

The validity of peer feedback is usually understood as the extent to which the comments produced by students identify the strengths and weaknesses that are actually present in a text. In practice it has most often been estimated by comparing the judgements of students with those of instructors, on the assumption that the latter provide an appropriate standard. Draycott et al. (2013), comparing the comments of 214 undergraduate students with those of six experienced instructors on a corpus of argumentative essays, found that the problems identified by peers corresponded to those identified by instructors in roughly 62% of cases, a figure which rose to 78% when only problems of organisation were considered. Agreement fell sharply, on the other hand, for problems of argumentation, where students tended to accept claims which instructors regarded as insufficiently supported. Even so, the authors concluded that, for most purposes, peer comments were sufficiently accurate to be useful.

The use of instructor judgements as the criterion of validity is not, however, without its critics. Nyborg (2011) points out that instructors themselves disagree substantially when asked to evaluate the same text, and that treating any single instructor as the standard simply relocates the problem. Teodorescu (2019) adopts a different perspective: while she accepts that agreement with instructors may be an acceptable indicator for holistic marks, she argues that it is inappropriate for formative comments, whose value lies in their capacity to prompt revision rather than in their conformity to an expert view. On this account, a comment which an instructor would not have made may nonetheless be valid if it leads the writer to clarify an argument. This position has considerable appeal, although it makes validity difficult to measure, since the effect of a comment can only be observed after the text has been revised, and revisions are seldom attributable to a single source.

Reliability, in the sense in which the term is used in the assessment literature, concerns the consistency of judgements: the degree to which different reviewers, or the same reviewer on different occasions, arrive at similar conclusions about the same text. Its importance for peer feedback is evident, since a student whose draft is read by a single peer has no way of knowing whether the comments received are typical or idiosyncratic. Mbatha and Ortlieb (2016), who asked 96 postgraduate students to rate the same four research proposals, reported inter-rater correlations ranging from 0.41 to 0.73, depending on the criterion considered. They caution that a single coefficient of this kind is a highly context-dependent indicator of agreement and ought not to be generalised beyond the conditions of the study. What is required, they suggest, is a better understanding of the reviewers’ frequently divergent, criterion-specific judgements under conditions resembling those of ordinary teaching.

It is frequently observed that the reliability of individual peer reviewers is lower than that of instructors, but that the reliability of the average of several peer reviewers may equal or exceed it. Kerrigan (2021) found that the mean rating of four peers correlated more strongly with the mean rating of two instructors than did the rating of either instructor with that of the other. This finding has been taken by some institutions as a justification for replacing instructor marking with peer marking in large courses. Such a conclusion does not follow. Reliability is a necessary condition of validity but not a sufficient one, and four reviewers who share the same misconceptions will agree with one another while being consistently wrong. Moreover, the gains obtained by averaging apply to marks, which can be combined arithmetically, but not to written comments, which cannot.

blocos.h2: Peer review, peer grading and co-assessment

blocos.p: In recent years a number of alternative terms have been proposed, each of which, it is commonly held, captures an aspect of the practice that ‘peer feedback’ leaves obscure. ‘Peer review’ is preferred by those who wish to emphasise the continuity between classroom activities and the evaluation of manuscripts submitted to journals (Vasilakis 2020). ‘Peer grading’ is used, chiefly in the literature on large online courses, to refer to arrangements in which students assign marks to one another’s work. ‘Co-assessment’, finally, designates arrangements in which students and instructors share responsibility for evaluation. Yet on closer inspection these terms either describe particular conditions under which peer feedback takes place or rename it without adding any new content.

The case of ‘peer review’ is instructive. Vasilakis (2020) argues that the term prepares students for the conventions of academic publication, in which they will eventually participate as authors and reviewers. The analogy, however, is imperfect. Reviewers of manuscripts are, at least in principle, experts in the field, whereas students reviewing the drafts of their classmates are by definition novices; moreover, editorial review is primarily concerned with deciding whether a text should be published, while classroom feedback is concerned with helping a text to improve. To call the latter ‘peer review’ therefore imports expectations of expertise and of gatekeeping which are foreign to its purpose. Saldanha-Pirie (2022) adds that students who are told they are acting as ‘reviewers’ tend to adopt a judgemental tone and to recommend rejection rather than revision, an effect which she attributes directly to the connotations of the term.

‘Peer grading’ and ‘co-assessment’ present a different difficulty. Both refer to the summative uses of peer judgement which, as noted above, Rhydderch et al. (2018) prefer to call peer assessment, and neither says anything about the comments that may or may not accompany the marks. The proliferation of labels is not merely a matter of taste. When studies of grading in online courses and studies of formative comments in writing seminars are grouped under different names, the findings of one are rarely brought to bear on the other; when, conversely, they are grouped under the same name without qualification, results obtained under one set of conditions are applied uncritically to the other. The inescapable conclusion is that ‘peer feedback’, qualified where necessary by an indication of whether a mark is involved, remains the most serviceable term.

If the term itself requires no replacement, the practice it designates clearly requires support. Quennell (2014) suggests that much of the disappointment expressed by instructors arises from confusing the concept of peer feedback with the conditions under which it is implemented, and that feedback which fails under one set of conditions may succeed under another. Five approaches to improving those conditions are frequently discussed in the literature: the use of rubrics, the anonymity of reviewers and writers, the organisation of feedback in successive revision cycles, the training of reviewers and the incorporation of self-assessment. Each is considered below in terms of its advantages and its limitations.

A rubric is a document which specifies the criteria by which a text is to be evaluated and, usually, describes the performance expected at each of several levels. Castelnau (2015) argues that rubrics give students a shared vocabulary for discussing writing and direct their attention away from surface errors towards organisation and argument, the features which unguided reviewers most often neglect. A further advantage is that rubrics make the expectations of the instructor explicit, so that the writer can interpret comments in relation to a known standard. In a comparison of two cohorts of a first-year writing course, Draycott et al. (2013) reported that the proportion of comments addressing argumentation rose from 18% to 41% after a rubric was introduced.

Rubrics are not, however, free of drawbacks. Detailed rubrics may encourage reviewers to treat evaluation as a checklist, ticking criteria without engaging with the text as a whole, and they can penalise unconventional drafts whose strengths fall outside the categories provided. Nyborg (2011) further observes that, owing to differences in prior instruction, students tend to interpret the descriptors of a rubric in widely different ways, so that a common instrument does not necessarily produce common judgements. It would therefore seem that rubrics improve the focus of peer feedback more reliably than they improve its consistency; put differently, they are better at telling reviewers where to look than at ensuring that they all see the same thing. Their value, moreover, depends heavily on whether students have been taught to apply them.

Anonymity may be applied to the reviewer, to the writer or to both. Its principal justification is that students who know the identity of the person whose text they are reading tend to soften their criticism, particularly when the writer is a friend or a classmate of higher standing (Ilunga and Sorvik 2012). Concealing identities is intended to reduce this social pressure and, at the same time, to lower the anxiety which many students report when their work is exposed to the judgement of peers. In a study involving 138 students in three sections of an academic writing course, Oyelaran (2010) found that reviewers in the double-blind condition produced 27% more critical comments than those in the named condition, although the comments were not judged by instructors to be more accurate.

Anonymity nonetheless carries costs. It prevents precisely the kind of dialogue which Bakhtiyari and Lund (2017) regard as the defining feature of feedback, since a writer cannot ask an anonymous reviewer what a comment means. It also removes a source of accountability: reviewers who cannot be identified may invest less effort, and some studies report a higher proportion of brief or perfunctory comments under anonymous conditions. In small seminars, moreover, anonymity is often illusory, since students readily recognise one another’s topics and styles. Some instructors have accordingly adopted a compromise, in which reviewers remain anonymous during the first round of comments and are identified only when the writer requests clarification.

Revision cycles organise feedback as a sequence of stages rather than a single event. In the arrangement described by Kerrigan (2021), students submit a first draft, receive comments from two peers, revise the draft, and then submit it again to the same reviewers, who are asked to judge whether their earlier comments have been addressed. The repetition is intended to make feedback consequential: reviewers see the effect of what they wrote, and writers know that their response to the comments will itself be examined. Kerrigan reported that the proportion of comments which led to a visible change in the text increased from about one third in the first cycle to more than half in the second.

The principal limitation of revision cycles is the time they require, as each additional stage lengthens the interval between the first draft and the final submission, and in courses of a single semester this could leave little room for more than two cycles. Teodorescu (2019) also notes that reviewers who are asked to evaluate a revised draft tend to focus on the comments they themselves made, overlooking new problems introduced during revision. She recommends that their task in the second cycle be redefined, so that they can assess the text as a whole rather than merely verifying the changes which their own suggestions produced.

Reviewer training rests on the assumption that the ability to give useful feedback is not innate but can be taught. Training programmes typically combine an explanation of the criteria, the joint analysis of sample texts, and the comparison of students’ comments with model comments prepared by the instructor. Mbatha and Ortlieb (2016) found that a training session of ninety minutes raised inter-rater correlations among postgraduate students from an average of 0.52 to 0.68, while Saldanha-Pirie (2022) reported that trained reviewers produced fewer comments on surface features and more suggestions which writers were able to act on.

The benefits of training are, however, unevenly distributed, and it is not yet clear how long they last. Students who already write well appear to gain most, whereas those who struggle with the conventions of academic writing may lack the knowledge needed to apply what they have been taught (Kerrigan 2021). Training also requires time from instructors, which partly offsets the reduction in workload that peer feedback was supposed to provide. Finally, if model comments are presented as the correct answer, training may teach students to imitate the instructor rather than to exercise independent judgement, albeit with gains in consistency that should not be underestimated.

Self-assessment asks students to evaluate their own drafts, usually with the same criteria they apply to the work of their peers, before or after receiving peer comments. Its advocates argue that it transfers the evaluative judgement developed through peer feedback to the student’s own writing, which is, after all, the ultimate purpose of the exercise (Ferrant 2006). When self-assessment precedes peer review, the comparison between a writer’s own judgement and that of the reviewers can reveal blind spots; when it follows, it encourages the writer to decide which comments to accept rather than accepting them all, although writers who lack confidence in their own judgement seldom do so without guidance and tend instead to adopt every suggestion they receive. Its limitation is the well-documented tendency of less proficient writers to overestimate the quality of their work: Vasilakis (2020) found that students in the lowest quartile of final marks rated their drafts, on average, more favourably than those in the highest quartile did. Self-assessment thus appears to depend on the very evaluative capacity it is meant to develop.

Peer feedback has become a fixture of writing instruction in higher education, and the reasons for its adoption are, for the most part, sound. The definitions reviewed above differ in emphasis but share a common core, and the alternative terms proposed in recent years either describe particular conditions of use or import connotations that are foreign to the formative purpose of the practice. Questions of validity and reliability, on the other hand, cannot be resolved by terminology. The evidence suggests that peer comments can be reasonably accurate and that the judgements of several peers can be as consistent as those of an instructor, but also that these outcomes depend heavily on the conditions under which feedback is given.

None of the five approaches considered here is sufficient on its own. Rubrics direct attention to the features that matter but do not ensure that criteria are interpreted consistently; anonymity encourages candour at the expense of dialogue; revision cycles make feedback consequential but demand time that many courses lack; training improves consistency but benefits some students more than others; and self-assessment presupposes the very judgement it is designed to cultivate. The approaches are best seen as complementary, each compensating for some of the limitations of the others. The need, it is argued here, is not for new names for peer feedback, nor for its replacement by instructor marking, but for the deliberate combination of conditions under which students can learn to give, and to use, comments of genuine value.

questoes.enunciado: Com base no título e no resumo, o tema do estudo reportado no texto é
alternativas: o feedback entre pares na escrita acadêmica: definições concorrentes, validade e confiabilidade, e formas de medi-lo.
o feedback docente na escrita acadêmica: definições concorrentes, validade e confiabilidade, e abordagens para aprimorá-lo.
o feedback entre pares na escrita acadêmica: definições concorrentes, validade e confiabilidade, e abordagens para aprimorá-lo.
o feedback entre pares na escrita acadêmica: os termos alternativos que o substituem, sua validade e as abordagens para aprimorá-lo.
o feedback entre pares na escrita acadêmica: definições concorrentes, validade e confiabilidade, e as razões para sua adoção.
questoes.explicacao:
O título dá o recorte: definitions, validity and approaches to improvement; o resumo detalha Competing definitions, validity and reliability e Five approaches intended to improve the quality of peer feedback. (c) reproduz os três eixos.

Cada distrator troca um único elemento. (a) troca “aprimorar” por “medir”: o texto discute a dificuldade de medir a validade (§7), mas as abordagens são para improve. (b) troca o agente: o objeto é o feedback entre pares, e o docente aparece só como critério de comparação. (d) inverte a tese sobre os termos: eles add little conceptual clarity, e a conclusão mantém peer feedback. (e) toma a parte inicial do resumo (the reasons why it has come to occupy a central place) pelo tema inteiro e deixa de fora as abordagens de aprimoramento.
questoes.dica: Quando as alternativas são quase iguais, compare-as elemento por elemento (objeto, recorte, verbo final) com o título e o resumo. A errada costuma trocar uma única palavra: o agente, o verbo (aprimorar × medir) ou a posição dos autores sobre um termo.

questoes.enunciado: No parágrafo 1, qual elemento NÃO é apresentado como vantagem do feedback entre pares?
alternativas: A formação, nos alunos, da capacidade de julgar a qualidade de um trabalho.
O contato com outras maneiras de organizar uma argumentação.
Uma sensibilidade maior àquilo de que o leitor precisa.
Um alívio no volume de trabalho dos estudantes, que deixam de depender só do professor.
Uma reescrita mais ampla dos próprios textos por parte de quem comenta os dos colegas.
questoes.explicacao:
A lista de benefícios (§1) inclui the development of evaluative judgement (a), the exposure of students to alternative ways of structuring an argument (b) e a greater awareness of the needs of a reader (c). (e) também está no §1, acrescentada por Ferrant (2006): students who give feedback tend to revise their own texts more extensively than those who only receive it.

(d) é o intruso por uma palavra: a redução da carga de trabalho é a dos docentes (a reduction in the workload of instructors who would otherwise be the sole source of comments on drafts), não a dos estudantes.
questoes.dica: Em questões de “NÃO”, confira cada alternativa com o trecho, inclusive quem é o beneficiado ou o agente. O intruso pode repetir quase toda a frase do texto e trocar só um participante (docentes × estudantes).

questoes.enunciado:
Nos parágrafos 3 a 5, o texto compara várias definições de feedback entre pares. Associe cada autor à ideia que lhe é atribuída.

  1. Ilunga and Sorvik (2012)
  2. Castelnau (2015)
  3. Oyelaran (2010)
  4. Rhydderch et al. (2018)
  5. Bakhtiyari and Lund (2017)
  • (  )Se o texto não muda, o que houve foi informação, e não feedback.
  • (  )Basta que um aprendiz emita um juízo sobre o texto de outro, haja ou não reescrita.
  • (  )Quando há nota que entra no cômputo final, a prática merece outro nome.
  • (  )Comentários trocados entre colegas de um mesmo curso, com vistas à reescrita do rascunho.
  • (  )Espera-se que quem escreveu replique, peça esclarecimentos e, se preciso, recuse sugestões.

Assinale a sequência correta.
questoes.explicacao:
1º item: Oyelaran (3), a remark which leaves the text unchanged is, in her terms, ‘information, not feedback’ (§3). 2º: Castelnau (2), any judgement about the quality of a text […] irrespective of whether a revision follows. 3º: Rhydderch et al. (4), wherever peer comments are accompanied by a mark which contributes to the final grade, the practice should be described as peer assessment (§4). 4º: Ilunga and Sorvik (1), the exchange of written or spoken comments on a draft between students enrolled in the same course, with the aim of informing its revision. 5º: Bakhtiyari and Lund (5), a conversation in which the writer is expected to respond, to ask for clarification and […] to reject the suggestions received (§5).

Nas alternativas erradas: (b) erra os itens 1, 2, 3, 4 e 5; (c) erra os itens 2 e 5; (d) erra os itens 1 e 3; (e) erra os itens 1, 2, 4 e 5.
questoes.dica: Em associações com paráfrases, procure no trecho original a palavra que distingue cada autor (irrespective, acted upon, mark, conversation) e só então compare com a frase em português. Não elimine alternativas a partir de um único item: elas trocam pares de autores parecidos.

questoes.enunciado: Os segmentos destacados em “[…] and it has been influential among instructors who regard the one-way transmission of comments as a residue of more traditional models of teaching” (§5) e “Bakhtiyari and Lund do not deny that such arrangements exist; they simply decline to call them feedback, a position which, if accepted, would exclude the majority of the practices they set out to describe” (§5) referem-se, respectivamente, a
alternativas: o relato de Bakhtiyari e Lund – grupos de escrita em que os rascunhos eram discutidos face a face – Bakhtiyari e Lund.
a conversa entre escritor e revisor – arranjos com comentários enviados por plataforma online e nunca discutidos – Bakhtiyari e Lund.
a conversa entre escritor e revisor – grupos de escrita em que os rascunhos eram discutidos face a face – as práticas.
a conversa entre escritor e revisor – arranjos com comentários enviados por plataforma online e nunca discutidos – as práticas.
o relato de Bakhtiyari e Lund – arranjos com comentários enviados por plataforma online e nunca discutidos – Bakhtiyari e Lund.
questoes.explicacao:
it é o sujeito coordenado a Their account draws on studies […]: é o relato (account) de Bakhtiyari e Lund que has been influential among instructors, não a conversation da frase anterior. such arrangements resume a frase imediatamente anterior: comments are typically submitted through an online platform, read by the writer some days later and never discussed; os grupos de discussão face a face são a base empírica do relato, justamente o oposto desses arranjos.

Nas alternativas erradas: (a) erra o item 2; (b) erra o item 1; (c) erra os itens 1, 2 e 3; (d) erra os itens 1 e 3.
questoes.dica: Para cada pronome, pergunte qual é o papel dele na oração (sujeito de quê? quem faz a ação?) antes de olhar o substantivo mais próximo. Um pronome sujeito de “set out to describe X” não pode ser o próprio X.

questoes.enunciado:
Sobre a validade do feedback entre pares, indique se os segmentos a seguir estão em acordo (A) ou desacordo (D) com o que apresentam os parágrafos 6 e 7.

  • (  )Ao confrontar os comentários de mais de duzentos alunos de graduação com os de meia dúzia de docentes experientes, Draycott et al. (2013) obtiveram coincidência em pouco mais de 60% dos casos.
  • (  )A coincidência entre alunos e docentes aumentou quando se consideraram só os problemas de organização e despencou nos de argumentação, em que os alunos aceitavam afirmações mal fundamentadas.
  • (  )Teodorescu (2019) aceita a concordância com docentes como indicador de validade para comentários formativos, mas a recusa para notas holísticas.
  • (  )Apesar dessa queda, Draycott et al. (2013) concluíram que os comentários dos pares eram suficientemente precisos para qualquer finalidade.

Assinale a sequência correta.
alternativas: A – A – A – A
A – A – D – D
D – D – A – A
A – D – A – A
D – A – D – D
questoes.explicacao:
1 (A): comparing the comments of 214 undergraduate students with those of six experienced instructors […] in roughly 62% of cases (§6). 2 (A): a figure which rose to 78% when only problems of organisation were considered. Agreement fell sharply, on the other hand, for problems of argumentation, where students tended to accept claims which instructors regarded as insufficiently supported.

3 (D): a posição está invertida. Teodorescu accepts that agreement with instructors may be an acceptable indicator for holistic marks, mas argues that it is inappropriate for formative comments (§7). 4 (D): o quantificador foi trocado: for most purposes (“para a maioria das finalidades”), não para qualquer finalidade.

Nas alternativas erradas: (a) erra os itens 3 e 4; (c) erra os itens 1, 2, 3 e 4; (d) erra os itens 2, 3 e 4; (e) erra o item 1.
questoes.dica: Itens em acordo costumam vir parafraseados (214 → “mais de duzentos”, six → “meia dúzia”); não os descarte por soarem diferentes. Nos itens em desacordo, confira quem aceita o quê e os quantificadores (most × any, some × all).

questoes.enunciado: O segmento destacado em “What is required, they suggest, is a better understanding of the reviewers’ frequently divergent, criterion-specific judgements under conditions resembling those of ordinary teaching” (§8) pode ser traduzido, no contexto em que é empregado, por
alternativas: os julgamentos do revisor, frequentemente divergentes e específicos de cada critério.
os julgamentos dos revisores, frequentemente divergentes e específicos de cada critério.
os revisores de julgamentos frequentemente divergentes e específicos de cada critério.
os julgamentos dos revisores, divergentes em cada critério e frequentemente específicos.
os critérios específicos dos julgamentos frequentemente divergentes dos revisores.
questoes.explicacao:
O núcleo é o último substantivo, judgements. O genitivo the reviewers’ (apóstrofo depois do s) indica plural: “dos revisores”. Os modificadores são frequently divergent (o advérbio modifica divergent) e o adjetivo composto criterion-specific (“específico de cada critério”).

(a) lê reviewers’ como singular (reviewer’s). (c) toma o possessivo como núcleo. (d) desloca frequently para specific e transforma criterion-specific em “divergentes em cada critério”. (e) faz de criterion o núcleo, quando ele é só parte do adjetivo composto.
questoes.dica: Em sintagmas nominais, ache o núcleo (o último substantivo antes do verbo ou da preposição), traduza-o primeiro e pendure nele os modificadores. Com possessivo, observe a posição do apóstrofo (reviewer’s = um; reviewers’ = vários); com adjetivo composto, o hífen une as duas palavras num só modificador.

questoes.enunciado:
Considere as seguintes afirmações sobre os termos alternativos discutidos nos parágrafos 10 a 12.

I - O termo peer grading circula sobretudo na literatura sobre cursos online de grande porte e designa situações em que os alunos dão notas aos trabalhos uns dos outros.II - Vasilakis (2020) atribui diretamente às conotações da palavra reviewer a tendência dos alunos a adotar um tom julgador e a recomendar a rejeição dos textos.III - Quando estudos sobre notas em cursos online e estudos sobre comentários formativos recebem nomes diferentes, os resultados de uns raramente são aproveitados pelos outros.IV - Em co-assessment, a responsabilidade pela avaliação é repartida entre alunos e docentes.

Estão em acordo com o texto
alternativas: apenas III e IV.
apenas II.
apenas I, II e III.
apenas I, III e IV.
apenas I e II.
questoes.explicacao:
I: ‘Peer grading’ is used, chiefly in the literature on large online courses, to refer to arrangements in which students assign marks to one another’s work (§10). III: When studies of grading in online courses and studies of formative comments in writing seminars are grouped under different names, the findings of one are rarely brought to bear on the other (§12). IV: ‘Co-assessment’, finally, designates arrangements in which students and instructors share responsibility for evaluation (§10).

II troca o autor: Vasilakis (2020) aparece no mesmo parágrafo, mas defende o termo peer review. Quem relata o tom julgador e o atribui às conotações do termo é Saldanha-Pirie (2022): an effect which she attributes directly to the connotations of the term (§11).

Nas alternativas erradas: (a) deixa de fora I, que está correta; (b) inclui II, que é falsa, e deixa de fora I, III e IV, que estão corretas; (c) inclui II, que é falsa, e deixa de fora IV, que está correta; (e) inclui II, que é falsa, e deixa de fora III e IV, que estão corretas.
questoes.dica: Em afirmações I-II-III, desconfie da que está quase toda certa: confira o autor, o grupo e o sentido do efeito. Se dois autores aparecem no mesmo parágrafo, verifique a qual deles a ideia pertence.

questoes.enunciado: A função do segmento destacado em “It would therefore seem that rubrics improve the focus of peer feedback more reliably than they improve its consistency; put differently, they are better at telling reviewers where to look than at ensuring that they all see the same thing” (§15) é
alternativas: reformular em outros termos a afirmação anterior sobre foco e consistência.
introduzir a conclusão que decorre das observações de Nyborg sobre os descritores.
acrescentar às rubricas uma limitação distinta da que foi apresentada antes.
exemplificar com um caso concreto a diferença entre foco e consistência.
atenuar o comprometimento dos autores com a afirmação anterior.
questoes.explicacao:
Put differently (“dito de outro modo”) anuncia que a mesma ideia será dita com outras palavras: “melhorar o foco” vira telling reviewers where to look, e “melhorar a consistência” vira ensuring that they all see the same thing. Nada de novo é acrescentado.

(b) é a função de therefore, no início da frase. (c) corresponde a moreover, na frase seguinte (Their value, moreover, depends heavily on…). (d) não se aplica: não há caso concreto, só uma reformulação genérica. (e) é a função de would […] seem, que atenua a primeira oração, não de put differently.
questoes.dica: Quando o trecho tem vários marcadores (therefore, would seem, moreover), atribua uma função a cada um antes de responder. Reformulação (in other words, put differently, that is to say) repete a ideia anterior com outras palavras; conclusão (thus, therefore) tira dela uma consequência.

questoes.enunciado:
Sobre o feedback anônimo, indique se os segmentos a seguir estão em acordo (A) ou desacordo (D) com o que apresentam os parágrafos 16 e 17.

  • (  )Quando nem revisor nem autor eram identificados, os comentários críticos foram pouco mais de um quarto mais numerosos do que na condição nominal.
  • (  )Além de mais numerosos, esses comentários foram considerados pelos docentes mais precisos do que os da condição nominal.
  • (  )Sob anonimato, alguns estudos registram comentários mais extensos, embora menos cuidadosos, porque os revisores não podem ser identificados.
  • (  )No arranjo de compromisso, o revisor permanece oculto na primeira rodada e só é revelado se o autor do texto pedir esclarecimentos.

Assinale a sequência correta.
alternativas: D – A – A – D
A – A – A – A
A – A – A – D
D – D – D – A
A – D – D – A
questoes.explicacao:
1 (A): reviewers in the double-blind condition produced 27% more critical comments than those in the named condition (§16); 27% é “pouco mais de um quarto”. 2 (D): although the comments were not judged by instructors to be more accurate. 3 (D): o texto fala em a higher proportion of brief or perfunctory comments under anonymous conditions (§17): comentários breves, não mais extensos. 4 (A): reviewers remain anonymous during the first round of comments and are identified only when the writer requests clarification.

Nas alternativas erradas: (a) erra os itens 1, 2, 3 e 4; (b) erra os itens 2 e 3; (c) erra os itens 2, 3 e 4; (d) erra o item 1.
questoes.dica: Nos itens A/D, confira a direção de cada detalhe (mais/menos, breves/extensos, primeira/segunda rodada). Um item com a causa certa e o efeito invertido continua em desacordo.

questoes.enunciado: Os segmentos destacados em “[…] and then submit it again to the same reviewers, who are asked to judge whether their earlier comments have been addressed” (§18) e “[…] and writers know that their response to the comments will itself be examined” (§18) referem-se, respectivamente, a
alternativas: os comentários dos dois colegas – os comentários dos revisores – o rascunho – os comentários dos dois colegas.
a resposta dos escritores – os escritores – os escritores – a resposta dos escritores.
o rascunho – os revisores – os escritores – a resposta dos escritores.
os comentários dos dois colegas – os revisores – o rascunho – os comentários dos dois colegas.
o rascunho – os revisores – os escritores – os comentários dos dois colegas.
questoes.explicacao:
it: os alunos revise the draft, and then submit it again, ou seja, reenviam o rascunho; os comentários foram recebidos, não reenviados. O primeiro their: os revisores julgam se os seus comentários anteriores foram atendidos (who are asked to judge whether their earlier comments…), e quem escreveu comentários foram eles, não os escritores. O segundo their: writers know that their response, a resposta dos escritores, não dos revisores.

Nas alternativas erradas: (a) erra os itens 1, 2, 3 e 4; (b) erra os itens 1 e 2; (d) erra os itens 1, 3 e 4; (e) erra o item 4.
questoes.dica: Pronomes reflexivos e enfáticos (itself, themselves) retomam o sujeito da própria oração, não o substantivo mais próximo. Para their, pergunte de quem é a coisa possuída: quem escreveu os comentários? quem dá a resposta?

questoes.enunciado: Assinale a alternativa cujo segmento sublinhado expressa recomendação (aquilo que é aconselhável fazer).
alternativas: “[…] the comments a student receives <u>may</u> depend less on the qualities of the draft than on who happens to be assigned to read it” (§2).
“They caution that a single coefficient of this kind is a highly context-dependent indicator of agreement and <u>ought not to</u> be generalised […]” (§8).
“[…] four reviewers who share the same misconceptions <u>will</u> agree with one another while being consistently wrong” (§9).
“She recommends that their task in the second cycle be redefined, so that they <u>can</u> assess the text as a whole […]” (§19).
“[…] in courses of a single semester this <u>could</u> leave little room for more than two cycles” (§19).
questoes.explicacao:
Ought not to equivale a should not: Mbatha e Ortlieb aconselham não generalizar o coeficiente (e o verbo caution, “advertir”, reforça o valor de recomendação).

(a) may e (e) could indicam possibilidade. (c) will indica previsão com alta certeza. (d) é a armadilha: a frase contém o verbo recommends, mas o sublinhado can está na oração de finalidade (so that they can assess) e expressa capacidade/possibilidade; a recomendação está em recommends […] be redefined, que não está sublinhado.
questoes.dica: Classifique o modal sublinhado, não a frase: possibilidade (may, might, could, can), certeza (will, must, cannot), recomendação ou obrigação fraca (should, ought to, had better, it is advisable). Uma palavra como “recommends” perto do sublinhado não muda o valor do modal.

questoes.enunciado: Assinale a alternativa cujo segmento sublinhado NÃO estabelece relação de CAUSA.
alternativas: “[…] the formative and summative functions are inseparable in practice, <u>given that</u> students who know that a mark is involved write comments of a different kind […]” (§4).
“Nyborg (2011) further observes that, <u>owing to</u> differences in prior instruction, students tend to interpret the descriptors of a rubric in widely different ways […]” (§15).
“In small seminars, moreover, anonymity is often illusory, <u>since</u> students readily recognise one another’s topics and styles” (§17).
“<u>Since</u> the first syntheses on the subject appeared in the mid-2000s, peer feedback has been incorporated into writing courses […]” (§1).
“The principal limitation of revision cycles is the time they require, <u>as</u> each additional stage lengthens the interval between the first draft and the final submission […]” (§19).
questoes.explicacao:
Em (d), since é temporal (“desde que”): marca o ponto de partida de um período, o que o presente perfeito has been incorporated e a data in the mid-2000s confirmam.

Nas demais há causa. (a) given that (“dado que”) explica por que as funções são inseparáveis. (b) owing to (“devido a”) dá a causa das interpretações divergentes. (c) aqui since é causal (“já que”): os alunos se reconhecem, por isso o anonimato é ilusório. (e) as (“uma vez que”) explica por que o tempo é a principal limitação; não é comparação nem tempo.
questoes.dica: Since e as têm mais de um sentido. Since + ponto no tempo, com presente perfeito na oração principal, é temporal (desde); since + motivo é causal (já que). As pode ser causal, temporal (enquanto) ou comparativo (como): teste a troca por because.

questoes.enunciado: No segmento “[…] it encourages the writer to decide which comments to accept rather than accepting them all, although writers who lack confidence in their own judgement seldom do so without guidance and tend instead to adopt every suggestion they receive” (§22), a expressão destacada retoma
alternativas: “to decide which comments to accept” (§22).
“accepting them all” (§22).
“to evaluate their own drafts” (§22).
“reveal blind spots” (§22).
“to overestimate the quality of their work” (§22).
questoes.explicacao:
Do so substitui uma ação já mencionada. A frase diz que os escritores inseguros raramente fazem isso sem orientação e, em vez disso (instead), adotam todas as sugestões: logo, o que eles não fazem é decide which comments to accept.

(b) é a leitura apressada (a ação mais próxima), mas é exatamente o que esses escritores fazem (adopt every suggestion they receive), e não o que raramente fazem. (c) é a definição de autoavaliação, no início do parágrafo; (d) é o efeito da autoavaliação feita antes da revisão por pares; (e) é a limitação apresentada depois, atribuída aos escritores menos proficientes.
questoes.dica: Do so, do the same e this/such + substantivo retomam uma ação ou ideia anterior. Substitua a expressão por cada candidato e leia a frase inteira: o restante dela (aqui, instead) costuma excluir a opção mais próxima.

questoes.enunciado:
Relacione cada abordagem (em inglês) ao efeito ou vantagem que o texto lhe atribui.

  1. Rubrics (§14–§15)
  2. Anonymous feedback (§16–§17)
  3. Revision cycles (§18–§19)
  4. Reviewer training (§20–§21)
  5. Self-assessment (§22)
  • (  )Diminui a tendência a abrandar as críticas quando se sabe quem escreveu o texto.
  • (  )Elevou a concordância entre avaliadores após uma única sessão de hora e meia.
  • (  )Fez crescer, de um grupo para outro, a parcela de comentários sobre argumentação.
  • (  )Ampliou, de uma etapa para a seguinte, a parcela de comentários que alteraram o texto.
  • (  )Pode revelar pontos cegos ao confrontar o julgamento de quem escreveu com o dos colegas.

Assinale a sequência correta.
questoes.explicacao:
1º: anonimato (2), students who know the identity […] tend to soften their criticism (§16). 2º: treinamento (4), a training session of ninety minutes raised inter-rater correlations […] from an average of 0.52 to 0.68 (§20). 3º: rubricas (1), In a comparison of two cohorts […] the proportion of comments addressing argumentation rose from 18% to 41% (§14). 4º: ciclos de revisão (3), the proportion of comments which led to a visible change in the text increased from about one third in the first cycle to more than half in the second (§18). 5º: autoavaliação (5), the comparison between a writer’s own judgement and that of the reviewers can reveal blind spots (§22).

Nas alternativas erradas: (a) erra os itens 3 e 5; (b) erra os itens 1 e 2; (d) erra os itens 1, 2, 3, 4 e 5; (e) erra os itens 1, 3, 4 e 5.
questoes.dica: Quando vários itens falam de “aumento de uma proporção”, ancore cada um no detalhe que só ele tem: duração da sessão, grupos comparados, etapas sucessivas. Resolva todos antes de escolher, porque as sequências erradas trocam só dois itens.

questoes.enunciado: Assinale a alternativa que NÃO corresponde a uma limitação que o texto atribui à abordagem indicada.
alternativas: Rubrics: podem prejudicar rascunhos pouco convencionais cujos méritos não cabem nas categorias previstas.
Anonymous feedback: em turmas pequenas costuma ser só aparente, pois os alunos reconhecem temas e estilos uns dos outros.
Revision cycles: na segunda rodada, os revisores tendem a se fixar nos próprios comentários e a deixar passar problemas novos.
Reviewer training: os ganhos são desiguais, maiores para quem já escreve bem, e não se sabe quanto tempo duram.
Self-assessment: os escritores mais proficientes tendem a avaliar seus rascunhos melhor do que eles realmente são.
questoes.explicacao:
(a) they can penalise unconventional drafts whose strengths fall outside the categories provided (§15). (b) In small seminars, moreover, anonymity is often illusory, since students readily recognise one another’s topics and styles (§17). (c) reviewers who are asked to evaluate a revised draft tend to focus on the comments they themselves made, overlooking new problems introduced during revision (§19). (d) The benefits of training are, however, unevenly distributed, and it is not yet clear how long they last. Students who already write well appear to gain most (§21).

(e) troca o grupo: quem superestima o próprio texto são os menos proficientes (the well-documented tendency of less proficient writers to overestimate the quality of their work, §22); os alunos do quartil mais alto avaliaram seus rascunhos de forma menos favorável.
questoes.dica: Quando o intruso não vem de outro parágrafo, procure a troca de um grupo ou quantificador (mais × menos proficientes, alguns × todos). Confira cada alternativa até o fim, mesmo a que começa igual ao texto.

questoes.enunciado: Qual alternativa sintetiza a CONCLUSÃO (§23–§24) a que chegam os autores do texto?
alternativas: Mantido o termo peer feedback, nenhuma abordagem basta sozinha, e o que se pede é combinar deliberadamente condições que se compensam.
As abordagens são complementares, e os autores propõem combiná-las e trocar peer feedback por um termo que indique se há nota envolvida.
Como a média de vários pares pode ser tão consistente quanto a de um docente, a correção docente pode ser dispensada em turmas grandes.
As abordagens se complementam, mas o treinamento de revisores é o que compensa as limitações de todas as demais.
As definições divergem sobre a natureza do processo, e só uma terminologia mais precisa resolverá os problemas de validade.
questoes.explicacao:
O §24 diz que None of the five approaches considered here is sufficient on its own, que elas são complementary, each compensating for some of the limitations of the others, e que a necessidade é not for new names for peer feedback, nor for its replacement by instructor marking, but for the deliberate combination of conditions. (a) reúne esses pontos.

(b) acerta a combinação, mas o §12 propõe manter peer feedback, apenas qualified where necessary by an indication of whether a mark is involved, não trocá-lo. (c) contradiz o §24 (nor for its replacement by instructor marking) e o §9 (Such a conclusion does not follow). (d) torna central uma abordagem que, segundo o §24, benefits some students more than others; a compensação é recíproca. (e) contradiz o §23: as definições share a common core, e validade e confiabilidade cannot be resolved by terminology.
questoes.dica: Na síntese da conclusão, desconfie da alternativa que começa certa e termina com uma proposta que os autores rejeitam. Confira cada parte contra uma frase específica do §23–§24.
